day-1.t: Day 1 - Saying hello, and how Turkish sounds

v: Say please, thank you and sorry
Read Turkish out loud without guessing

b.v: Every letter has one sound and keeps it. Read a Turkish word the way it is written and you have said it correctly. There is nothing like the English through, though and thought.

v: g = always hard, as in go

b.v: Two letters look unfamiliar but are easy. The i without a dot is written ı and sounds like the a at the end of sofa. The ğ is never pronounced on its own - it just stretches the vowel before it, so dağ (mountain) comes out as daa.

v: Hoşça kalın = Goodbye, said by the one leaving
Güle güle = Goodbye, said by the one staying

b.v: Those last two are not interchangeable. The person walking out says hoşça kalın (stay well). The person staying says güle güle (go smiling). Say the wrong one and people will smile at you.
3) The words you will use most
Teşekkür ederim is a mouthful at first. Turks often shorten it to teşekkürler, and nobody minds.

v: İyiyim, teşekkür ederim = I'm well, thank you

b.v: Siz is the polite you. Use it with anyone you have just met, anyone older, and anyone serving you. Turkish has a familiar form too, which comes on day 3.
Say this conversation out loud twice.|Merhaba! Nasılsınız?|İyiyim, teşekkür ederim. Siz nasılsınız?|Ben de iyiyim. Teşekkürler.|Hoşça kalın!|Güle güle!

v: Read the six greetings out loud five times
Learn which goodbye belongs to who
Say teşekkür ederim until it stops feeling long

day-2.t: Day 2 - Numbers, and asking what things cost

v: Ask a price and understand the answer

b.v: 2) Turkish numbers are built, not memorised
After ten there is nothing new to learn. You glue the words together in the order you say them in English, with no and, no hyphen, and no surprises.

v: on bir = eleven, literally ten one

b.v: One hundred is just yüz, never bir yüz. Same with bin. But two hundred is iki yüz.

v: kuruş = the small coin, a hundred to a lira
Bu ne kadar? = How much is this?

b.v: A real exchange in a shop.|Affedersiniz, bu ne kadar?|Elli lira.|Çok pahalı. Kırk lira?|Tamam, kırk beş.|Tamam, aldım. Teşekkür ederim.
Aldım means I'll take it, literally I took it. Turkish often uses the past where English uses the present - the decision is made, so it is done.
After a number, the noun stays singular. Two teas is iki çay, never iki çaylar. The number already told you there were two.

v: Count out loud from one to twenty
Say your phone number in Turkish
Practise kaç para and çok pahalı

day-3.t: Day 3 - Talking about yourself, and siz against sen

v: Say your name, where you are from and what you do
Know when to use siz and when to use sen
Say I am, you are, this is

b.v: Turkish has two words for you, and picking the wrong one is the fastest way to sound rude or oddly stiff.

v: siz = polite, or more than one person
sen = familiar, one person you know well

b.v: Use siz with strangers, shopkeepers, officials, anyone older, and anyone at work. Use sen with friends, children, and family. If you are unsure, use siz - being slightly formal is never insulting, but sen to the wrong person is.
Turks often say sen diyelim, meaning let's use sen. That is an invitation to relax. Wait for it rather than assuming it.
Turkish has no separate word for am or is. The ending on the word carries it.

v: Siz Ayşe misiniz? = Are you Ayşe?
Ben doktorum = I am a doctor

b.v: Notice there is no word for a. Ben doktorum is I am doctor, and that is correct Turkish.

v: Türkçe bilmiyorum = I don't speak Turkish
Biraz Türkçe biliyorum = I speak a little Turkish

b.v: The ending -lı turns a place into a person from there. Pakistan becomes Pakistanlı, Lahor becomes Lahorlu. Which vowel you use depends on the word, and that is tomorrow's lesson.

v: o = he, she, it - all one word

b.v: Turkish has no he or she. O covers both. Nobody will ever mistake a gender in Turkish because the language does not mark it.
Introduce yourself.|Merhaba, ben Khalid.|Nerelisiniz?|Pakistanlıyım. Siz nerelisiniz?|Ben İstanbulluyum.|Memnun oldum. (Pleased to meet you.)|Ben de memnun oldum.

v: Say your own introduction out loud, three times
Decide which you would use with a shopkeeper, a friend, and a manager
Learn memnun oldum - you will use it constantly

day-4.t: Day 4 - Vowel harmony, the rule behind everything

v: Pick the right vowel without memorising each word

b.v: About 25 minutes. This is the most important lesson in the course.

Both mean the plural - houses and books. So why is one -ler and the other -lar? Because Turkish endings copy the vowel sound of the word they join. This is vowel harmony, and once you see it, half of Turkish grammar stops being memorisation.
Every Turkish vowel belongs to one of two groups, decided by where your tongue sits.

v: Front vowels: e, i, ö, ü
Back vowels: a, ı, o, u

b.v: Look at the last vowel of the word. If it is from the front group, the ending uses e. If from the back group, the ending uses a.

v: ev (house), last vowel e, front = evler
kitap (book), last vowel a, back = kitaplar
göz (eye), last vowel ö, front = gözler
okul (school), last vowel u, back = okullar

b.v: Say them out loud. Your mouth will tell you when it is right long before your brain does - that is exactly why the rule exists. Turkish endings follow the path of least effort.
Some endings have four shapes instead of two, using ı, i, u or ü. The same logic applies, just finer.

v: after a or ı use ı
after e or i use i
after o or u use u
after ö or ü use ü

b.v: You met this yesterday without knowing. Pakistanlıyım has ı because Pakistan ends in a. İstanbulluyum has u because İstanbul ends in u.
Make these plural, then check.|ev - evler|kitap - kitaplar|çiçek (flower) - çiçekler|masa (table) - masalar|gün (day) - günler
Do not add the plural after a number. Beş kitap, not beş kitaplar. Turkish thinks the number has done that job already.

v: Sort these by front or back: ev, kitap, okul, göz, araba, şehir
Say each one out loud and listen for whether it flows
Say I want and I would like

b.v: Çay is the national drink and arrives in a small tulip glass. It is offered constantly, in shops as much as cafes, and refusing the first glass is normal but refusing three in a row looks cold.

v: Bir çay istiyorum = I want a tea
Bir çay lütfen = A tea please
Çay var mı? = Do you have tea?

b.v: Var and yok do enormous work in Turkish. Var means there is or it exists; yok means there isn't. You will hear yok twenty times a day.
Ordering in a lokanta.|İyi günler. Ne var?|Çorba, tavuk, balık var.|Bir tavuk ve bir ayran lütfen.|Tabii. Başka bir şey?|Hayır, teşekkür ederim.|Afiyet olsun.
Afiyet olsun is said before you eat and after you finish - it means may it do you good. The reply when someone has cooked for you is elinize sağlık, health to your hands.

v: Kartla ödeyebilir miyim? = Can I pay by card?
Order a full meal out loud, starting from İyi günler
Learn var and yok until they come without thinking

day-6.t: Day 6 - Verbs, and saying what you do

v: Say what you are doing now

b.v: That is the dictionary form, like to go in English. Which one it takes is vowel harmony again - front vowels get -mek, back vowels get -mak.
This is the biggest change from English. Turkish puts the verb at the end of the sentence, always. Ben çay içiyorum is literally I tea drink.

v: Ben çay içiyorum = I am drinking tea
O eve gidiyor = He is going home
Biz ekmek alıyoruz = We are buying bread

b.v: Read a Turkish sentence to the end before deciding what it means. The verb at the end can change everything, including whether it is a negative.
Drop the -mek or -mak, add -iyor, then the personal ending. The vowel in -iyor follows harmony: -ıyor, -iyor, -uyor or -üyor.
Slip -mi- in before the ending. It harmonises too: -mı-, -mi-, -mu-, -mü-.
Bilmiyorum is probably the single most useful word in this course. Learn it before anything else on this page.
Say each one, then make it negative.|Çay içiyorum - Çay içmiyorum|Eve gidiyorum - Eve gitmiyorum|Türkçe biliyorum - Türkçe bilmiyorum

v: Say five things you are doing right now
Use the endings for to, from and in

b.v: English puts a small word in front. Turkish puts an ending on the back. Same job, opposite end.
Place names take an apostrophe before the ending. Ordinary nouns do not. İzmir'de, but okulda.
Stopping someone in the street.|Affedersiniz, eczane nerede?|Düz gidin, sonra sağa dönün.|Uzak mı?|Hayır, çok yakın. Beş dakika.|Çok teşekkür ederim.
Gidin and dönün are the polite command forms - go, turn. With sen they would be git and dön.

v: Burada inecek var = Someone is getting off here
Ask where five different places are
Practise eve, evde, evden until the difference is automatic

b.v: Pazar means Sunday and also market. Pazartesi is the day after Pazar, and Cumartesi the day after Cuma. The names tell you the order.

v: Saat kaç? = What time is it?
Üç çeyrek geçiyor = Quarter past three
Dörde çeyrek var = Quarter to four

b.v: Notice geçiyor means passing and var means there is. Quarter past is a quarter passing; quarter to is a quarter remaining. Turkish counts towards the hour.
Fixing a meeting.|Yarın müsait misiniz?|Evet, müsaitim. Saat kaçta?|Saat ikide olur mu?|Olur. Nerede?|Ofiste. Görüşürüz.
Olur mu? means will that do? and Olur means that works. Two of the most useful words in daily Turkish.

v: Ocak, Şubat, Mart = January, February, March
Nisan, Mayıs, Haziran = April, May, June
Temmuz, Ağustos, Eylül = July, August, September
Ekim, Kasım, Aralık = October, November, December
Say today's day and date in Turkish
Tell the time five times through the day
Ask who, what, why and how

b.v: 1) The little word that makes a question
English changes the word order to ask. Turkish adds mi as a separate word at the end, and harmonises it: mi, mı, mu, mü.

v: Çay var mı? = Is there tea?
Bu iyi mi? = Is this good?

b.v: Mi is written as a separate word but pronounced joined on. It is never capitalised and never starts a sentence.

v: Ne zaman geliyorsunuz? = When are you coming?
Nasıl gidiyoruz? = How are we going?
Anladım = I understand, I got it
Tekrar eder misiniz? = Could you say that again?
İngilizce biliyor musunuz? = Do you speak English?
Ne demek? = What does that mean?
Nasıl denir? = How do you say it?

b.v: Anlamıyorum and yavaş lütfen will carry you through most of your first month. People slow down happily when asked.
Turn each into a question.|Çay var - Çay var mı?|Bu ucuz - Bu ucuz mu?|Türkçe biliyorsunuz - Türkçe biliyor musunuz?|Otel yakın - Otel yakın mı?

v: Yardım eder misiniz? = Could you help me?
Telefonum yok = I have no phone
Hold a short conversation start to finish
Review everything from the ten days
Introduce yourself and say where you are from
Order food and ask for the bill
Say what you are doing, and what you are not
Ask where something is and follow the answer
Tell the time and arrange to meet
Ask questions and say you did not understand
Endings harmonise with the last vowel of the word
The verb goes at the end of the sentence
Endings replace English prepositions - eve, not to house

b.v: Everything else in Turkish is built on these three. When a new ending appears, check its vowel against the word, and it will make sense.

Read it through twice, then cover the page and say it.|Merhaba! Nasılsınız?|İyiyim, teşekkür ederim. Siz?|Ben de iyiyim. Nerelisiniz?|Pakistanlıyım. İstanbul'da çalışıyorum.|Ne kadar zamandır buradasınız?|İki yıldır.|Türkçeniz çok iyi!|Teşekkür ederim, biraz biliyorum.

v: var / yok = there is / there isn't
The past tense - geçmiş zaman - opens up telling stories
The possessive endings: evim, evin, evi - my, your, his house
Listen to Turkish radio or a series with subtitles, even if you catch one word in ten

b.v: You will be understood long before you are correct. Turks are generous with anyone trying their language, and a wrong ending has never stopped anyone getting a cup of tea.

v: Hold the day 10 conversation without looking
Write five sentences about your own day
Take the quiz and claim your certificate
